source: FRI (2026-07-16) AI models have likely reached parity with superforecasters: what the top systems do
finding: Only coarse method descriptions are public. Cassi AI: multi-stage pipeline. It writes sub-questions and search queries, retrieves context, filters for relevance and recency, runs an ensemble of models, and a further LLM reads the reasoning to give the final forecast. Torchcast: proprietary multi-agent system that mixes its own trained models with commercial LLMs. xAI and Google DeepMind: no method given. The post gives no tokens, cost or ablations.
numbers: p vs supers (one-sided bootstrap): Cassi 0.41, xAI 0.16 and 0.15, DeepMind 0.14. Market questions: Cassi and one anonymous ensemble rank above the superforecaster median. Dataset parity since May 2026. Tournament lag 50 days; preliminary board needs 225 resolved dataset questions.
limits: Read through a summarising fetch tool; the result tables are images and were not readable. Supers last elicited 2024; CIs overlap; parity not outperformance.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is only partly closed: the pipeline shape is known (decompose, retrieve, filter, ensemble, supervise) but compute is not.

source: ForecastBench wiki: How to submit, How does it work, FAQ (FRI)
finding: The submission rules set no limit on tokens, tools, retrieval sources or ensemble size, and require no disclosure of them. Fields are only organization, model name, optional reasoning, and an ensemble flag (model='ensemble'). Each set has 500 questions (250 market, 250 dataset). Market questions get one forecast; dataset questions up to 8 horizons. Missing forecasts are imputed at 0.5. Max 3 submissions per team per round. The crowd forecast given to LLMs is the market value frozen 10 days before the due date.
numbers: Question sets every 2 weeks since 2024-07-21; freeze D-10; due D 23:59:59 UTC. Leaderboard needs 95% coverage and (tournament) 225 dataset plus 50 market resolved questions; 50-day lag. Human set is 200 questions, a subset of the LLM set.
limits: Pages for crowd forecasts, retrieval limits and token counts were explicitly silent. Question and resolution files are not public (licences), so outside replication of the full set is not possible.
agent_relevance: Equal-token comparison of leaderboard entries cannot be done from public data. Our own harness must log tokens per question.

source: ForecastBench wiki Changelog (FRI), entries 2025-02 to 2026-10
finding: The benchmark itself changed many times, so trend and parity lines mix different tests. 2025-10-07: difficulty-adjusted Brier with two-way fixed effects; only resolved market questions scored; missing market forecasts imputed 0.5 (earlier imputation of market value called overly generous). 2025-10-17: combination questions dropped, 1000 to 500 questions. 2026-03-04: Brier Index. 2026-05-20: baseline market difficulty by fixed effects because models lack context past cutoff. 2026-08-05: RAND Forecasting Initiative source ended. 2026-08-19: Kalshi added. 2026-09-30: dataset horizons cut from 8 to 5 (7, 30, 90, 180, 365 days).
numbers: 3 submissions per team (2025-11-19); at least 50 resolved market questions per round (2026-03-05); market sampling stratified (2026-02-19).
limits: No entry on leakage. The changelog lists changes only; effect sizes are not given.
agent_relevance: Report horizon-wise and per-source results; do not compare a 2025 number with a 2026 number without checking the scoring version.

source: Cassi AI leaderboard page and founder blog (Feb and Jul 2026)
finding: Vendor pages show the parity claim is close, not a win. On the Jul 2026 board the superforecaster median is still rank 1 (Brier Index 69.2) and Cassi-2026-05-10 is rank 2 (68.8, Brier 0.097). The earlier entry ensemble_2_crowdadj scores 66.5 (Brier 0.112) and is rank 13. In Feb 2026 that entry scored 0.102 vs supers 0.086. The pipeline, models and cost are not disclosed; the entry name suggests an ensemble adjusted by the crowd forecast.
numbers: Feb 2026 sample: 955 resolved dataset and 170 market questions; dataset questions at 8 horizons but only up to about one month had resolved. Cassi 1st of 269 on ForecastBench (vendor figure).
limits: Vendor source with a commercial interest. Scores on the vendor page come from different resolved sets. The blog post does not describe the pipeline.
agent_relevance: Even the top system improved from 0.102 to 0.097 Brier within months by changing entries: scaffold changes are measurable at about 0.005 per version.

source: FRI (2025-10-08) How well can large language models predict the future? (ForecastBench update)
finding: This is the likely source of the brief's Nov 2026 parity date. Superforecasters 0.081 vs best LLM (GPT-4.5) 0.101, a gap of 0.020. Linear extrapolation at about 0.016 Brier per year gave overall parity in November 2026 (95% CI Dec 2025 to Jan 2028). Market-question parity March 2026, dataset-question parity June 2026. On market questions LLMs copy the market: GPT-4.5 correlates 0.994 with it and gave exact market values on 26 of 122 questions.
numbers: Market Brier slope 0.015/yr (tournament), 0.036/yr (baseline without crowd or tools). GPT-4 0.131 to GPT-4.5 about 0.03 gain. Public median fell from rank 2 to rank 22.
limits: GPT-4.5 shares no questions with the 2024 superforecasters, so the gap is extrapolated through intermediate models. Authors say the last mile may be hardest.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a large part of LLM market-question accuracy is the supplied price. Also corrects K25: the November 2026 date does exist in an FRI source.

source: FRI (2026) Making forecasting scores easier to interpret: introducing the Brier Index
finding: Source of the 0.017 figure. Superforecasters Brier 0.086 (Index 70.6%) vs best LLMs (Cassi ensemble_2_crowdadj, xAI Grok 4.20 Preview) 0.103 (67.9%): gap 0.017 Brier, 2.7 Index points. Index rose 2.4 points from Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) to Grok 4.20 Preview (Oct 2025). This post extrapolated parity to March 2027 (Brier; CI Feb 2026 to Jan 2028) or May 2027 (Index).
numbers: Brier Index = (1 - sqrt(Brier)) x 100; 50% = always 0.5.
limits: Fetched page gave no date and did not describe the difficulty adjustment. The Karger Table 26 7-day gap is also 0.017, so the two coincide.
agent_relevance: The brief's 0.017 is real but from this post, not only from Karger Table 26. Parity dates: Nov 2026 (Oct 2025 post), Mar 2027 (this post), already reached for several systems in Jul 2026 (x01).

source: Murphy (2026) Agentic forecasting with structured linguistic beliefs (BLF): comparison to Cassi, Grok 4.20, Foresight-32B and a no-LLM crowd baseline
finding: First paired test of leaderboard agents against a crowd-plus-prior baseline. On 400 ForecastBench question-date instances (791 resolution events), a baseline that only submits the market price (market questions) and the empirical base rate (dataset questions) scores Brier Index 69.9. BLF (Gemini 3.1 Pro agent) gets 73.3, and is the only method to beat the baseline significantly overall (+3.4). Cassi +1.0, Grok +1.9 to +1.4, Foresight -1.5 (all ns). On market questions BLF is only +2.3 over the price (ns, 200 events). Gains come mostly from dataset questions (+4.5).
numbers: Market BI: crowd alone 81.5, BLF 83.8, Cassi 82.0, Grok 79.5, Foresight 81.0. Dataset BI: prior alone 58.3, BLF 62.7, Cassi 59.6. Paired bootstrap, 5000 resamples. Question difficulty explains 62% of score variance.
quote: the only compared method to significantly outperform a crowd+empirical-prior baseline in terms of overall performance
limits: Backtest on two tranches (2025-10-26 and 2025-11-09), not live. Grok scored only tranche A and Foresight only B. Author built BLF, so possible tuning advantage. Market comparisons lack power.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: on market questions the supplied price is nearly the whole answer at this sample size. Our agent should be judged against a price-only baseline.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF, Appendix A.5 compute and Table 5 costs
finding: Rare public compute figure for a ForecastBench-level agent. Up to 10 steps, 10 minutes, 1 to 8 minutes per question. Five trials over 400 question-date instances use 50 to 100 million tokens, mostly input. One method on the full A+B set costs about 250 USD with context caching (about 1000 USD uncached). Roughly 125k to 250k tokens per question over 5 trials (derived by this reader: 50-100M divided by 400). Three LLMs: main agent, a cheap filter, a cheap summariser; an agent with 10 steps and 10 results per step needs 100 summariser calls.
numbers: Gemini 3.1 Pro 2/12 USD per million tokens in/out; Gemini 3 Flash 0.50/3 for filtering and summaries. 50 parallel workers: 1 to 3 hours wall clock for 5 trials x 400 questions.
limits: Author estimate for own system. Derived per-question tokens are this reader's arithmetic, not stated in the paper. Cassi, xAI and DeepMind compute still unknown.
agent_relevance: Sets a reference budget: about 0.6 USD and 0.1M-0.25M tokens per question for a leaderboard-level agent.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF ablations: belief state, trial averaging, Platt and hierarchical calibration, LLM aggregation
finding: Component effects are small and backbone-dependent. A structured belief state (probability plus evidence summary carried across steps) raised Brier Index by 3.00 (Pro) and 1.99 (Flash) but gave -0.42 (n.s.) for GPT-5.4. More trials (K up to 5) helped a little; shrinkage tuned by cross-validation collapsed to plain logit averaging. Platt scaling gave +0.72 (with crowd) and +1.48 (without crowd) BI, hierarchical +0.98 and +1.80, but the author found no statistically resolved overall gain for the Pro backbone in the historical comparison. An AIA-style LLM aggregator that reads the reasoning traces did worse than a simple mean on this benchmark. Markov memory vs full history: +2.40 BI favouring Markov, CI [-0.17, 4.36].
numbers: Table 3: Pro market +5.34 [3.32, 7.72], dataset +0.67; Flash market +4.06; GPT market -0.62. 400 instances; 5000 paired resamples.
limits: One author, one benchmark, backtest. Kimi K2.5 results omitted because failed runs defaulted to 0.5 (market submission rate 6.2% vs 82.4%): pipeline reliability can masquerade as quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 8: calibration gains shrink when a strong anchor (market price) is already given. Count submission failures when ablating scaffolds.

source: Murphy (2026) BLF, Appendix B: leakage audit of date-filtered search
finding: Four-layer leakage defence (date-filtered Brave search, LLM leak classifier, tool date clamping, URL blocking), then a second LLM audit of 2,272 search results from tranche A. Runtime filter caught 320 of 341 leaks (93.8% recall) but dropped 577 clean results (29.9% false positives). Only 21 of 1,377 results the agent saw were leaks (1.5%). At least one flagged result appeared for 14 of 200 tranche-A questions (7.0%), or 14 of 76 web-search questions (18.4%). Parametric leakage cannot be ruled out; cutoffs were used only as a selection rule.
numbers: Confusion matrix: clean kept 1354, clean dropped 577, leak kept 21, leak dropped 320.
limits: Second-LLM verdicts, not human-verified. Exposure rate does not measure effect on the forecast.
agent_relevance: Leakage is small but not zero in careful backtests; live questions avoid it entirely.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: ensemble size, supervisor, and statistical-correction tables
finding: Read the tables behind the recipe. Ten sampled forecasts averaged: 0.1140 vs 0.1182 for one random forecast (FB-7-21; size curve on 1610 MarketLiquid questions, returns diminish after a handful). Mean, trimmed mean and median are equal (0.1140, 0.1142, 0.1138). Supervisor: agentic supervisor 0.1125, non-agentic 0.1168, pick-best-of-k 0.1191, no supervisor 0.1199. Corrections: Platt fitted in-distribution (leave-one-out) 0.1071, fitted out-of-distribution on Halawi's set 0.1104, fixed log-odds extremising with coefficient 3 0.1085, none 0.1119 (ID column) and 0.1125 (OOD column); raw mean 0.1140. Platt coefficient sqrt(3)=1.73 beats superforecasters even when their own coefficient is tuned (1.72); tuned optimum for AIA is 2.27.
numbers: Platt on the arithmetic mean of k forecasts gave the lowest Brier. Supervisor Top@3 33.9%, outperform-all 3.8%.
limits: Company report. Costs and tokens not given. Components were added in sequence on one benchmark, not ablated at equal compute. Column labels of Table 11 were garbled in text extraction; values paired by this reader.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 8: extremising transfers across question sets with about 60% of the in-distribution gain (0.1125 to 0.1104 vs 0.1119 to 0.1071). A fixed sqrt(3) is a safe default only for hedging models.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster, section 5.2: foreknowledge-bias audit
finding: An LLM judge flags search results that reveal post-cutoff outcomes. Validation on 502 traces by hand: 16 true leaks (3.2%), 65 false positives (12.9%), 412 true negatives (82.1%), 9 false negatives (1.8%). Estimated about 1.65% of all search results contain some foreknowledge. Date filters on search providers fail because article dates are hard to determine. The authors bound the effect rather than remove it.
numbers: n=502 manual audit; flag precision 16/81 = 20%; recall 16/25 = 64% (derived).
limits: Low precision; unflagged runs are trusted. Company report.
agent_relevance: Backtest numbers need a leak rate attached. Prefer live or frozen-corpus tests.

source: Liptay, Schwarz, Poyiadzi, Wildman, Bosse (2026) Evaluating strategic reasoning in forecasting agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Frozen-corpus pastcasting at scale: 1,417 questions asked Oct 2025 and resolved Dec 2025, with about 15 million documents (8.7 million unique) searched offline. It detects Brier differences of 0.004. Frontier agents with simple prompt: Opus 4.6 0.131, Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.143, GPT-5.4 0.151, Grok 4.20 Beta 0.165 (differences 0.012 to 0.033, all significant). Typical agent: 10-20 tool calls, 5-6 minutes, 80k-200k input and output tokens, 50-300 snippets, 5-20 pages read, 0.14 USD (Grok) to 0.55 USD (Opus) per question. Authors state agents did better than agents with live web access. Claude Opus 4.7 (cutoff Jan 2026) appeared to use post-Oct-2025 knowledge.
numbers: Gemini 3.1 Pro vs 3.0 Pro on same research: 0.129 vs 0.138, CI [0.002, 0.016]. Calibration/refinement: Opus 0.005/0.073, Grok 0.003/0.039 (best calibrated, worst refined). On 200 hard questions, Opus had all 8 rollouts correct on 18%, none on 45%.
limits: Same vendor builds the benchmark and the best forecaster. Only 2 months of resolution window. Fidelity of the frozen corpus to the live web is checked only by the older 20-question test (d19).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 5: gives a real tokens-and-cost figure and a parametric-leak warning for models with later cutoffs. Our agent tests should use a frozen corpus and exclude models whose cutoff passes the question date.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) BTF-2: the state-of-the-art forecasting agent versus single agents and a mean of four
finding: A multi-run, multi-step pipeline beat every single agent, but the paper does not ablate it. Brier on 1,367 questions: SOTA agent 0.119 at 1.68 USD per question; Opus 4.6 0.130 (0.55 USD, two runs identical); Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.141 (0.30); GPT-5.4 0.152 (0.24); mean of the 4 agent runs 0.125. The five listed ingredients: mean of several runs, forecasts of related questions, recalibration on historic calibration curves, asking a longer-scope version of the question first, and detecting and correcting biases in rationales. By this reader's sum, the four-agent mean costs about 1.64 USD, close to the SOTA agent's 1.68 USD, and is 0.006 worse.
numbers: Delta vs SOTA: Opus 0.011 [0.006, 0.017], mean of 4 0.007 [0.002, 0.011]. Calibration term SOTA 0.002 vs Opus 0.005; refinement 0.081 vs 0.075.
limits: No per-ingredient numbers. Cost sum of the four-agent mean is derived by this reader (the paper gives per-agent cost only).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 9: at roughly equal cost, extra structure (related-question context, recalibration, bias checks) beat plain multi-model averaging by about 0.006. Not a clean test, since the compute split differs.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) BTF-2: prompt with forecasting guidance, pre-mortem, and base-rate failure modes
finding: Prompt guidance helps one model and not another. With the same pre-gathered research and no search, Gemini 3.1 Pro with the long forecasting-tips prompt scored 0.129 vs 0.141 with a simple prompt. The Opus 4.6 agent that does its own research scored 0.131 under both prompts (read from a table whose layout was garbled). The stronger forecaster's rationales stress pre/post-mortem analysis, other perspectives and wildcards far more than single agents. Human experts reviewed 130 worst cases: 24 had significant strategic errors, including extrapolating base rates too strictly after a process had changed and falling back to a conservative prior after a good forecast.
numbers: Judgment over fixed evidence: Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.141, Opus 4.6 0.153, GPT-5.4 0.156, Grok 4.20 0.163 (N=1417). Providing others' research hurt the Opus agent: 0.131 to 0.153.
limits: Rationale-emphasis analysis was scored by an LLM on one structure; the authors say it is subjective. No test of base-rate-first or frequency framing.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no 2026 test confirms base-rate-first. A base-rate step can anchor too hard when the process is disrupted; pair it with a disruption check and a pre-mortem.

source: Aitchison, Jeen, Shevlane, Day (2026) Diversity is the Strength of the AI Crowd: design and limits
finding: At a fixed number of samples, not tokens, the best mix is not all from one model. N=113 binary Metaculus AI Benchmark Q2 2025 questions resolved May-July 2025; 5 forecasters (Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5, Grok 4, Kimi K2.5, fine-tuned gpt-oss-120b), 3 samples each, same retrieval-then-predict scaffold. All 101 allocations at budget B=5 were scored. Best team: 2 fine-tuned, 1 each Gemini, GPT-5, Grok. Removing Grok 4 costs 1.7 baseline points, fine-tuned 0.6, Gemini or GPT-5 less than 0.1 each. Moving along the GPT-5/Gemini edge gains at most 0.6 points, toward the fine-tuned vertex 2.7.
numbers: Optimum for the three-model mix (FT, Gemini, GPT) = (0.56, 0.26, 0.18). Pairwise Jensen-Shannon divergence used for diversity. Probabilities clipped at 0.05.
quote: the strength of the AI crowd comes not from sampling more forecasts indiscriminately, but from combining forecasts across models with complementary errors
limits: Authors list: single tournament, 113 questions, at most 3 runs per model, per-sample cost ignored. No bootstrap intervals. The optimum was picked on the same questions that scored it (selection effect among 101 allocations).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 half answered: equal samples, not equal tokens. Mix model families, but treat the exact weights as unproven.

source: Paleka et al. (2024/25) Consistency checks for language model forecasters: ArbitrageForecaster and correlation table
finding: Re-read for gap 7. Consistency correlates with Brier only for some checks, and not stably. Table 2 correlations of arbitrage violation with Brier: Negation 0.60 (scraped set) but -0.36 (NewsAPI set); Paraphrase 0.57 and 0.13. Conditional checks reached R above 0.9. The authors built ArbitrageForecaster that patches a base forecast by arbitraging related questions. It improved the checks it was trained on, but did not generalise to held-out checks or improve forecasting. They warn consistency as a training metric could be gamed (forecasting 50% passes Paraphrase, Negation and ExpEvidence). Part of the correlation is that stronger models are better at both. They could not reproduce Halawi's system (news API deprecated), so no retrieval-based forecaster was tested.
numbers: Benchmark of 3,000 consistency checks for questions resolving in 2028. Forecasters with Brier worse than 0.25 excluded. MMLU error vs Brier correlation 0.38 and 0.55 for comparison.
quote: this improvement does not generalize to other held-out consistency checks, nor does it improve the actual forecasting performance
limits: Few forecasters, mostly 2024 models without search. Nothing tests consistency as a within-question sample selector.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 mostly answered no for the optimisation use: use conditional and negation checks as an audit, not as a target to patch or a sample picker.

source: Chandak, Goel, Prabhu, Hardt, Geiping (2026) Scaling open-ended reasoning to predict the future (OpenForesight): consistency, retrieval and leakage control
finding: Uses a static monthly news snapshot instead of web search, retrieving only articles up to one month before resolution, because search engines leak through updated articles. Over 40% of selected generated questions leaked the answer even after prompts told the writer to avoid it; leakage removal was needed before training helped. Training Qwen3 8B with a Brier-plus-accuracy reward cut arbitrage violations by 15% on Paleka's long-horizon checks (44% on some) as a side effect, and held-out testing May to August 2025 matched much larger proprietary models.
numbers: Reward = accuracy + adapted Brier score; accuracy-only hurt calibration, Brier-only hurt exploration.
limits: Open-ended questions, not ForecastBench binary questions. Training method, out of scope for a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Consistency improved as a by-product of calibration training, not as a selection signal at inference. Frozen retrieval snapshots are the model to copy for our tests.

source: FutureSearch, Wildman et al. (2025) Bench to the Future: live-versus-retro fidelity check
finding: The only check that frozen retrieval matches live search is small. 20 open questions, 20 runs per question for each of three agents, in both live and retro (frozen) mode. Forecast distributions looked alike by eye, and no more different than for the no-evidence control, except one question (NFL tush push ban) where news broke between scraping and the live run. Retro forecasts sometimes had higher variance. The authors argue model ranking stays meaningful if all agents see comparable information.
numbers: 299 questions in BTF 1; effective sample about 178.8 after down-weighting correlated questions.
limits: Visual comparison, no score or rank correlation. BTF-2 adds scale but not a live check.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: no study shows that a frozen-corpus score predicts the live ForecastBench rank.

source: Li, Wang, El Lahib, Xia, Pi (2026) Simulated ignorance fails
finding: Telling a model to forget what it knows after a cutoff does not work. Across 477 competition-level questions and 9 models, instructions leave a 52% performance gap between simulated and true ignorance; chain-of-thought does not suppress prior knowledge even when traces show no post-cutoff mention; reasoning-optimised models show worse fidelity. Authors recommend against retrospective forecasting set-ups based on prompted ignorance.
numbers: 477 questions, 9 models, 3 intervention layers (abstract numbers; body read in part).
limits: Competition questions rather than ForecastBench; only the abstract and Figure 2 text read in full.
agent_relevance: Back-tests must use models whose training ended before the question date. A system prompt saying pretend it is date X is not a control.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Prophet Arena: temporal analysis, markets versus LLMs by lead time
finding: Re-read the horizon section for gap 10. Market baseline Brier falls as resolution nears. Markets lag several frontier LLMs when forecasts are made far in advance and overtake them close to resolution (hours), when news arrives. Authors warn raw Brier across horizons mixes skill with difficulty, and that forecasts too close to resolution should be excluded.
numbers: Models shown: GPT-5R, Grok 4, Claude Sonnet 4R, Gemini 2.5 Flash R, Llama 4 Scout vs the market. Lead-time bins from over 4 days to 0-3 hours; values only in a figure.
limits: 2025 models; the newest 2026 models were not tested. Figure values were not readable in text.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open for 2026 models. Report score by lead time against the market, not pooled.

source: Metaculus FutureEval / AI Benchmark page (2026): costs, effort and what separates bots
finding: Tournament-level compute facts. Cost per question across bots runs about 0.10 to 3 USD, from about 50 USD to over 1,000 USD per season. Strong model choice is called the biggest success differentiator, with no numbers. Of 9 top-10 bots that answered the Spring 2026 survey, 5 spent at least two full-time weeks. 60 questions can separate best from worst but not good from slightly better. A bot ranked 41st of 50 rose to 12th in the last days. Titles of research reports include Pros Beat Bots, but the Gap is Nearly Gone (Spring 2026); their bodies were not reachable.
numbers: Seasonal tournaments 300-400 questions; MiniBench about 60 questions per round. Bot-maker survey Spring 2026, n=46.
limits: Secondary summary through a fetch tool; the Pros Beat Bots report itself was not found and not read.
agent_relevance: Our test sets need hundreds of questions; 60 is noise-limited. A budget of about 1 USD per question matches the top bots.

source: IBM Think (2026) AI forecasters: a new opportunity for business, hire humans too (secondary)
finding: Secondary news piece on the parity result. More than 35 organisations on the ForecastBench board, over half small prediction-focused firms. Cites a Metaculus report that agentic search, simulation on history and consensus of several model answers together equal about nine months of base model progress. No single winning strategy.
numbers: 35+ organisations.
limits: Journalism; the Metaculus report behind the nine-month figure was not found or opened. Treat the figure as a pointer, not evidence.
agent_relevance: If base-model progress is about 0.016 Brier per year (d05), nine months is about 0.012 Brier (derived).

source: Karkar and Chopra (2025) Future is unevenly distributed: forecasting ability depends on what we ask
finding: Small study on 392 filtered market questions from Jan-Jul 2025 (150 sampled, 25 per category). Adding up to ten time-bounded news snippets helped some categories (finance, sports) and hurt others (politics, geopolitics), with failure modes called rumour over-weighting, definition drift and recency bias.
numbers: 392 questions after filtering; 6 categories x 25 questions; metrics accuracy, Brier, ECE.
limits: Very small per-category samples, no search agent; per-category numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 side evidence: raw news in the prompt can hurt; the retrieval step needs a relevance filter.
